findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Narrow the 'failed override is still refused' claim to failures before the reset. After the heal, have heal_superseded_clone check that the replay finished (no staged leftovers, no un-replayed fresh events), and add a test that injects a _replay failure.
evidence: src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py:102-118 — update-ref and reset --hard run before _replay
src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py:190-213 — _replay's update-index/checkout/commit raise StaleOverrideError on failure
src/rebar/_store/sync.py:156-168 — StaleOverrideError is caught and the function still returns True
findings.finding: The plan says a superseded clone that the heal could not move because of a 'failed override' is still refused as DIVERGED. That holds only for failures before the reset. override_onto_reclaimed_remote runs update-ref (backup), then `reset --hard` onto the remote commit, and only then _replay (update-index/checkout/commit). _replay can raise StaleOverrideError after the clone has already moved. _override_if_reclaimed catches that error, logs it, and returns True. The retry then passes the precheck, because merge-base now succeeds, and commits on the baseline. The fresh unpushed events were not replayed (they exist only under the backup ref), and replay blobs staged before the failure may still be in the index.
findings.location: Approach — 'or a superseded clone the heal could not move (fetch failure, busy lock, unreadable horizon config, failed override), is still refused as DIVERGED'
scenarios: Replay commit fails (e.g. index.lock contention or hook/env issue) after the reset: the retried write succeeds, but the clone's in-horizon unpushed events silently miss the remote
Partially staged replay entries are swept into the retried event's commit

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a regression test where the heal cannot move the superseded clone (e.g. write lock held, or fetch made to fail): the write is refused as DIVERGED, local HEAD is unchanged, and the remote tip is unchanged.
evidence: "a superseded clone the heal could not move (fetch failure, busy lock, unreadable horizon config, failed override), is still refused as DIVERGED"
Testing lists only successful-heal cases plus "A baseline whose lineage names another epoch is still refused"
findings.finding: The plan has no test for a superseded clone that the heal cannot move. The Approach promises that such a clone (fetch failure, busy lock, unreadable horizon config, failed override) is still refused as DIVERGED. Its key safety property, that no event is committed on the superseded history, is unproven. The Testing section only covers successful heals and an unrelated-lineage remote.
scenarios: Heal fails because another process holds the write lock; the retry path regresses and commits on the superseded tip, then push recovery loops on merge conflicts (the rejected-fix failure mode).
findings.suggested_fix: In test_write_after_reclaim.py, hold the write lock from a second handle (or point the remote URL at a nonexistent path after the fetch) and assert: CommandError with the DIVERGED message, `git rev-parse HEAD` unchanged, and the remote ref unchanged.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a test where the clone is superseded but the heal cannot move it (write lock held by another holder, or origin unreachable): the write is refused, the heal is attempted exactly once, and neither clone nor remote moves.
evidence: Testing lists happy-path comment, older-than-horizon comment, transition, and unrelated-lineage refusal only.
Approach: 'a superseded clone the heal could not move (fetch failure, busy lock, …) is still refused as DIVERGED'; 'retry the write once … a second refusal propagates.'
findings.finding: Two branches have no test: the heal-failure branch (heal cannot move a superseded clone, e.g. busy write lock or failing fetch, so the write is still refused) and the retry-once/second-refusal contract. The plan specifies both behaviours. The only refusal test covers the unrelated-lineage case, which never invokes the heal.
scenarios: A regression where the wrapper loops, or swallows the second refusal, or where a held write lock deadlocks the heal, would pass the suite.
findings.suggested_fix: In the new module, hold the store write lock from a second handle (or point origin at a removed path) on a superseded clone. Assert that `rebar.comment` raises a refusal, that the clone tip is unchanged, and that no stale-override backup ref was created.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the Cause section: emit_cross_session_warning reaches show_ticket/ensure_fresh only when warnings.cross_session is on and a session id resolves, and MCP suppresses it entirely. Pin those settings in the regression fixture so the control case is deterministic.
evidence: src/rebar/_commands/cross_session.py:46-54 — returns None before show_ticket unless config.warnings.cross_session and an acting session are both present
src/rebar/_lib_warn.py:52-53, 68-108 and src/rebar/mcp_server.py:514 — the MCP registrar runs every tool under suppress_cross_session_warning, so emit_cross_session_warning is a no-op there
src/rebar/_lib_reads.py:59 — show_ticket is the only route to ensure_fresh from this path
findings.finding: The Cause section says the library write reaches sync.reconverge 'via emit_cross_session_warning → show_ticket', and that the MCP write was skipped only because it was inside the 60 s throttle window. The code says otherwise. cross_session_warning_for calls show_ticket only when warnings.cross_session is enabled AND resolve_session_id() returns a value. Also, the MCP server wraps every tool in suppress_cross_session_warning, so emit_cross_session_warning returns immediately on MCP. An MCP write therefore never reaches reconverge through this route, whatever the marker's age.
findings.location: Cause (reproduced) — 'the library write runs via emit_cross_session_warning → show_ticket'
scenarios: MCP server whose clone was fetched to the reclaimed ref: no write ever heals through this route, not just writes inside the 60 s window
Library caller with warnings.cross_session off or no session id: the 'marker absent ⇒ write succeeds' reproduction does not hold
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the 'Why the CLI write healed' paragraph to say that the library/MCP write path has no guaranteed reconverge (cross-session read is opt-in and suppressed under MCP), and in test_write_after_reclaim.py explicitly disable warnings.cross_session (or unset the session id) so the write path is provably the first code to see the superseded ref.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Either run heal_superseded_clone before the plan-review/completion gates' store_freshness check, or add 'gated start-work/claim and gated closes' to the Out list. Make the transition regression test state its ticket type and gate configuration explicitly.
evidence: src/rebar/_commands/transition.py:307-313 — gates.plan_review_precheck runs for any cascade into in_progress before close_ticket → transition_core
src/rebar/_commands/claim.py:156 — plan_review_precheck runs before txn.claim_core (claim.py:184)
src/rebar/llm/plan_review/attest_gate.py:146-155 — claim_gate_check refuses with STALE_VERDICT when store_freshness is not fresh
src/rebar/_store/freshness.py:91-92 — _ref_divergence returns ('diverged', 0) when merge-base fails, i.e. exactly the superseded case
src/rebar/_commands/gates.py:204-214 — the plan-review close gate refuses the same way
findings.finding: The plan says wrapping transition_core and claim_core heals a superseded clone for transitions and claims, and that the write-path precheck is the first code to see the superseded ref. For start-work transitions and claims on plan-review-gated types, that is false. transition_compute (target in_progress) and claim.py both call gates.plan_review_precheck first. That reaches attest_gate.claim_gate_check, which calls store_freshness. store_freshness reports 'diverged' for unrelated histories and refuses with stale-store before transition_core/claim_core run. The plan-review close gate (gates.py:204) and the completion close gate behave the same way. The plan leaves gate-read freshness (store_freshness) out of scope, but its Out list does not say that gated claims/starts and gated closes keep failing.
findings.location: Approach — 'transition_core / claim_core through a typed heals_superseded_store decorator'; Scope — 'Also out: gate-read freshness (store_freshness)'; Testing — 'rebar.transition open → in_progress on a superseded clone lands on the remote'
scenarios: Box MCP server claims a story/epic after a reclaim: the claim gate refuses with stale-store DIVERGED, and the new decorator on claim_core never runs
The regression test passes only because its ticket type is exempt or the gate is disabled, which hides the production gap

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reuse `reads.ensure_fresh(tracker, force=True)` or `sync.reconverge` without a new wrapper for the heal, or state in the plan why a new wrapper is needed (for example the writer's lock budget versus `_RECONVERGE_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 2`), and state whether the heal honours the `sync.pull` opt-out.
evidence: reads.py:217 `def ensure_fresh(tracker: str, *, no_sync: bool = False, force: bool = False)` — docstring: "Every failure is swallowed … ``force`` skips only the throttle's age check … the opt-outs, the marker write and the best-effort contract are unchanged."
reads.py:245 `if _sync_disabled(cfg_root): return`, and reads.py:275-278 wraps `_store_sync.reconverge` in a try/except that swallows every exception
doctor.py:221 `def _reconverge(tracker)` → `sync.reconverge(tracker)` (another existing thin wrapper)
Plan: "The heal is the existing `sync.reconverge` round … It is best-effort and never raises"
findings.finding: The new `_store/freshness.py::heal_superseded_clone(tracker)` is planned as a best-effort, never-raising wrapper around `sync.reconverge`. The codebase already has such wrappers. `reads.ensure_fresh(tracker, force=True)` skips the 60 s throttle, swallows every failure, and also honours the `sync.pull` opt-out (`_sync_disabled`) and the local-read context. `doctor._reconverge` is another thin wrapper. The plan does not say why neither can be reused. A new wrapper that calls `sync.reconverge` directly would fetch even when the user has turned off `sync.pull`, which ensure_fresh respects.
findings.location: Approach — bullet 'run `_store/freshness.py::heal_superseded_clone(tracker)` … It is best-effort and never raises'
scenarios: A user with `sync.pull` disabled hits a superseded refusal. The new heal fetches and resets the clone anyway, while every read path deliberately leaves the clone alone.
Callers end up with three slightly different 'best-effort reconverge' entry points (reads, doctor, freshness), each with its own lock budget and opt-out behaviour.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Move the heal-and-retry boundary so that caller-side validation and state reads (require_id, require_not_ghost, current_tags, etc.) run again on the reclaimed baseline after the heal, or have the retried append re-check that the ticket exists and refuse if it does not, and add a regression test where the commented ticket's CREATE is discarded by a stale override.
evidence: Plan: 'Apply it to ... `_seam.append_event` (wrapping composition and commit, so the retried event is composed after the clone moved)'
src/rebar/_commands/leaf.py:76-84 — comment() calls require_id(ticket_id, tracker) and require_not_ghost(resolved, tracker) before append_event(...)
src/rebar/_commands/leaf.py:112-116 — tag() reads current_tags(resolved, tracker) to decide the no-op before append_event
src/rebar/_commands/_seam.py:458-554 — append_event/_append_event_body compose and commit without re-checking that the ticket exists
src/rebar/_store/stale_override.py:98-115 — a stale clone (oldest unpushed event older than the horizon) replays nothing, so locally created tickets vanish from the working tree after the reset
Plan Testing bullet 2 combines an older-than-horizon unpushed event with a new comment but does not cover the case where that event is the commented ticket's CREATE
findings.finding: The heal-and-retry wraps `_seam.append_event`, but the verbs that call it do their validation and derive state from the superseded store BEFORE append_event runs, and the retry never re-runs those checks. `leaf.comment` runs `require_id` and `require_not_ghost`, and `leaf.tag` computes `current_tags` for its idempotency no-op, all outside append_event. After `_override_if_reclaimed` moves the clone, the retried append composes an event for a ticket that may no longer exist on the new baseline. For example, the ticket's CREATE was an unpushed event older than the horizon, and the override discarded it into the backup ref. The retried event then pushes an orphan event (a ghost ticket) to the shared remote. Similarly, a TAG_DELTA or other state-derived payload can be computed from history the heal just replaced.
findings.location: Approach — `_seam.append_event (wrapping composition and commit, so the retried event is composed after the clone moved)`
scenarios: An MCP server creates ticket T (unpushed, older than the horizon), the remote is reclaimed, then comment_ticket(T): require_not_ghost passes on the old tree, the heal discards T's CREATE, and the retried COMMENT is pushed as an orphan event under T/ with no CREATE on the shared store.
tag(T, x) where the superseded clone's view of T's tags differs from the reclaimed baseline: the no-op/write decision was made against history the heal discarded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that heal_superseded_clone runs the reconverge round unconditionally, ignoring the 60 s throttle marker, and say whether it re-stamps the marker afterwards.
evidence: "The heal is the existing `sync.reconverge` round: fetch, take the write lock, `_override_if_reclaimed`"
"That reconverge is throttled to once per 60 s by a marker file."
Tests stamp "the read-path throttle marker ... as just-run"
findings.finding: The plan does not say whether heal_superseded_clone bypasses the 60 s reconverge throttle marker. The Cause section says reconverge is throttled to once per 60 s by a marker file, but not whether that check lives in reads.ensure_fresh or inside sync.reconverge itself. If it lives in reconverge, the heal would be a no-op in exactly the MCP scenario, where the marker was just stamped. The plan also does not say whether the heal re-stamps the marker.
scenarios: Long-running MCP server inside the 60 s window gets SupersededStoreRefused; the heal calls a throttled reconverge that returns immediately and the retry refuses again.
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the heal bullet: "heal_superseded_clone calls the reconverge round directly, bypassing the read-path throttle check; on success it stamps the marker."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify that heal_superseded_clone logs its outcome (moved / replayed N / discarded M backed up at <ref> / failed with reason), and that a refusal after a failed heal includes the heal failure reason in the error message.
evidence: "It is best-effort and never raises; a second refusal propagates."
"the old event is kept under the stale-override backup ref"
findings.finding: Heal outcomes are not surfaced to the write caller. The heal is "best-effort and never raises", so a failed heal yields a plain DIVERGED refusal with no reason. A successful heal past the horizon silently discards unpushed events into refs/rebar/stale-override/. Before this change those writes refused; after it, the write succeeds and the caller (e.g. an MCP client) gets no indication that local events were dropped.
findings.location: Approach — retry_after_superseded_heal bullet; Testing horizon case
scenarios: An MCP user's comment succeeds while an older unpushed transition is moved to a backup ref with no notice in the tool response.
An operator sees DIVERGED after a busy-lock heal failure and resets the clone by hand, as in the original incident.
findings.suggested_fix: Have heal_superseded_clone return a result (moved, replayed, discarded, backup_ref, failure_reason). Log it at warning level when events were discarded or the heal failed. When the second refusal propagates, append failure_reason to the DIVERGED message.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that the code wrapped by retry_after_superseded_heal/heals_superseded_store performs no externally observable side effects before the precheck, or name which ones are repeated on retry and why that is acceptable.
evidence: "raises `SupersededStoreRefused` ... before anything is committed"
"they reduce fresh state under the lock on the retry"
findings.finding: The plan does not state that the region retried by heals_superseded_store has no side effects before the precheck refuses. If transition_core/claim_core run hooks, cross-session warnings, or other observable work before finalize_event's refusal, the retry repeats them. The plan only states that nothing is committed.
scenarios: A transition emits a notification or cross-session warning on the first attempt, the precheck refuses, and the retry emits it again.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the failure-disposition contract per heal arm: unrelated remote = permanent DIVERGED; busy lock / fetch failure = retryable (distinct message or exit code, or an explicit retry hint); unreadable horizon / failed override = permanent, needs investigation.
evidence: 'raises `SupersededStoreRefused` (a `CommandError` subclass, same message and exit code)'
'It is best-effort and never raises; a second refusal propagates.'
Problem section: 'The MCP clone had to be reset by hand.'
findings.finding: Transient heal failures surface as the hand-reset-implying DIVERGED refusal, masking a retryable condition. The plan lists the heal-failure arms (fetch failure, busy lock, unreadable horizon config, failed override) and says each is 'still refused as DIVERGED' with 'same message and exit code'. That message says the store has 'DIVERGED from the shared store with no shared ancestor', which in the incident led to a hand reset. A busy lock or a network fetch failure is transient: retrying later would heal. The plan never states, per arm, whether the caller sees a retryable or a permanent disposition.
findings.location: Approach — 'An unrelated remote … or a superseded clone the heal could not move (fetch failure, busy lock, unreadable horizon config, failed override), is still refused as DIVERGED.'
scenarios: The MCP server writes while an idle-sync round holds the write lock. The heal is skipped for the busy lock, and the agent receives DIVERGED / 'no shared ancestor' and resets the clone by hand, though a retry seconds later would succeed.
A transient network failure during the heal's fetch is reported with the same permanent-sounding exit code as a genuinely unrelated remote.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep DIVERGED for the unrelated-lineage verdict. When the verdict is superseded but the heal could not move the clone, raise a distinct message, e.g. 'store superseded by reclaim; heal deferred (lock busy / fetch failed) — retry'. Map the transient arms to a retryable disposition.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State that `heal_superseded_clone` invokes reconverge unthrottled (ignoring the 60 s marker), and whether it stamps the marker on success.
evidence: 'That reconverge is throttled to once per 60 s by a marker file.'
'Also out: gate-read freshness (`store_freshness`) and the 60 s read throttle.'
findings.finding: The plan does not say whether `heal_superseded_clone` bypasses the 60 s reconverge throttle, or whether it stamps the throttle marker. The Cause section blames the throttle for skipping the reconverge, and the heal is described as 'the existing `sync.reconverge` round'. If the marker check lives inside `reconverge` (not only in `reads.ensure_fresh`), the heal no-ops in exactly the long-running-MCP case it targets. If the heal does not stamp the marker afterward, the next read may run a redundant second reconverge.
findings.location: Approach — 'The heal is the existing `sync.reconverge` round'; Scope — 'Also out: … the 60 s read throttle.'
scenarios: The MCP server reads constantly, so the marker is always fresh. The heal calls a throttled reconverge, which returns immediately, the retry refuses again, and the bug persists.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State how a write that triggered the heal surfaces discarded unpushed events to its caller (e.g. reuse the existing 'clone moved onto reclaimed remote' log line or a warning), and document it in `docs/concurrency.md`.
evidence: '`_override_if_reclaimed`, which backs the tip up under `refs/rebar/stale-override/`, resets onto the reclaimed baseline and replays fresh unpushed events.'
No stated warning or return field informing the write caller.
findings.finding: A plain write (e.g. `comment_ticket`) can now implicitly trigger the stale-clone override. The override moves older-than-horizon unpushed events to `refs/rebar/stale-override/` and drops them from the live store. The write then returns success, and the plan says nothing about surfacing that to the write's caller (CLI, MCP or library). Before this change the override ran only on a sync/read round, so a write never changed prior unpushed events as a side effect.
findings.location: Approach — `retry_after_superseded_heal`; Testing — 'the old event is kept under the stale-override backup ref'
scenarios: An MCP agent comments successfully. An earlier unpushed transition older than the horizon is moved to the backup ref, and the agent never learns its earlier work left the live store.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Use one mechanism for the superseded heal-and-retry (either the `heals_superseded_store` decorator on all three writes, or inline calls to `retry_after_superseded_heal`), not both.
evidence: Plan: "New `_commands/_seam.py::retry_after_superseded_heal(write, tracker)`" AND "`_commands/txn.py::transition_core` / `claim_core` through a typed `heals_superseded_store` decorator"

grep `functools.wraps` in src/rebar/_commands → no matches. grep `ParamSpec` in src/rebar → only `_cli/_parser.py:23`. No decorator pattern of this kind exists in `_commands` yet, so this would be the first.
Call sites: `append_event` (_seam.py:458), `transition_core` (txn.py:333), `claim_core` (txn.py:393). That is three users split across two mechanisms.
findings.finding: The plan adds two separate retry mechanisms for three call sites. `retry_after_superseded_heal(write, tracker)` wraps `append_event`, and a separate `heals_superseded_store` decorator wraps `transition_core` and `claim_core`. Each wrapper form has three or fewer users, and either form alone could cover all three. `append_event` takes `tracker` as a positional parameter just like `tracker_dir` in the txn cores, so one decorator would work for all three. Inline calls to the helper would also work.
findings.location: Approach — bullets 'New `_commands/_seam.py::retry_after_superseded_heal`' and 'Apply it to … through a typed `heals_superseded_store` decorator'
scenarios: A future write path (for example completion_txn or delete, both deferred in Scope) gets the heal. The maintainer has to choose between two equivalent wrappers, and the retry-once and second-refusal-propagates behaviour can drift between them.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep only `retry_after_superseded_heal(write, tracker)` and call it from inside `append_event`, `transition_core` and `claim_core`, wrapping each function's existing body. Alternatively, keep only the decorator and apply it to all three. Either way, drop the second form.
